Dear Diary,
Today I felt weird. I don't know how else to say it. At lunch Bhavna sat with the new girl instead of me, and my stomach went tight like a fist. Then my throat felt hot. Mummy asked at dinner, 'Are you angry? Sad?' I said, 'No, just weird.' She asked if I was jealous. I said no. I don't think I was. Or maybe a bit? It's like having a word stuck on your tongue, but for a feeling.
I drew it instead: a grey scribble with a knot in the middle. Mummy said that was a good picture of it.
Tomorrow I'll sit with Bhavna and the new girl.
— Minakshi

The night before Tomas moved to another city, Tuan, nine, couldn't eat his noodles. He pushed them round the bowl in their kitchen in Brisbane.
"Not hungry?" his dad asked.
"I feel weird."
"Weird how? Sick?"
Tuan shook his head. He put his hand flat on his stomach. "Here. Like it's full of stones. And here." He touched his throat. "It's tight."
"Are you sad about Tomas?"
Tuan frowned. "I don't know. Not sad like crying. Just... weird."
"Nervous? Worried?"
"I don't know!" Tuan's voice went high, and he put his head down on the table.
His dad stopped asking. He just rubbed Tuan's back. "It's okay not to know the word yet."

qa.q: What did Tuan push round the bowl?
qa.a: He pushed his noodles round the bowl.

qa.q: Why does Tuan's voice go high when his dad offers more words?
qa.a: He is frustrated because he really does feel something strong, but none of the words fits and he cannot explain it.

qa.q: What did Tuan's dad do well once Tuan got upset, and why did it help?
qa.a: He stopped offering words and rubbed Tuan's back, telling him it is okay not to know the word yet, which took the pressure off.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel the same night about moving away?
qa.a: Tomas might also feel a tight, strange mix of sadness and nerves about leaving Tuan, even if Tomas can't name it either.

It was Pranav's third week at the residential school in the hills. At nine at night he knocked on the hostel warden's door.
"Pranav? Everything okay?" asked Vidya Ma'am.
"I feel weird."
"Come sit. Weird where?"
He pointed at his chest and then his stomach. "It goes round and round. At night mostly."
"Does it feel like when you're hungry? Or scared? Or when you miss someone?"
Pranav, eleven, thought hard. His eyes went to the phone on her desk. "I don't know. It's just weird."
Vidya Ma'am didn't push. "Tell you what. Every night this week, come and tell me where it is and what it's like. We'll find the words together."
Pranav nodded. The round-and-round feeling was still there, but it seemed a little smaller.

qa.a: He pointed at his chest and then his stomach.

qa.q: What might Pranav's glance at the phone suggest about his feeling?
qa.a: It might suggest he feels homesick and wants to call his family, even though he can't put that feeling into words.

qa.q: Why was Vidya Ma'am's plan a helpful step?
qa.a: Instead of naming the feeling for him, she offered to meet each night to describe it together, which gives Pranav time and support to find his own words.

qa.q: How might Vidya Ma'am see Pranav's visit?
qa.a: She likely sees a new boy struggling with something like homesickness and trusts him enough not to force a label on him.
